content.text:
For a **typical cold**, there’s no medicine that “cures” it—most colds are viral and get better on their own, usually within **7–10 days**. Treatment is mainly to **relieve symptoms**. Antibiotics don’t help a common cold. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**If you’re an adult**, common options include:

- **Fever, headache, body aches, sore throat:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help. Follow the label, and avoid ibuprofen/NSAIDs if you’ve been told not to take them due to kidney disease, stomach ulcers/bleeding risk, blood thinners, etc.
- **Stuffy nose:**  
  A **saline nasal spray/rinse** is safest. A **decongestant** may help, but avoid or ask a clinician first if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems, or take certain antidepressants.
- **Cough:**  
  Honey can soothe cough in adults and children over 1 year old. Some OTC cough medicines may help a little, but benefits are often limited.
- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  An antihistamine may help, but can cause drowsiness or dry mouth.

**Important safety tips:**
- Don’t combine multiple “multi-symptom” cold products without checking ingredients—many contain **acetaminophen**, and too much can be dangerous.
- **Children:** OTC cough/cold medicines are **not recommended for children under 6** by CDC; FDA says not to use cough/cold products in children under 2, and many products are labeled not for under 4. Ask a pediatrician/pharmacist first. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))
- Don’t give **honey to babies under 1 year**.

**Get medical advice urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, dehydration, symptoms that worsen after initially improving, fever lasting more than 3 days, very high fever, severe sinus/ear pain, or if you’re at higher risk—pregnant, elderly, immunocompromised, or have asthma/COPD/heart disease.

If you tell me your **age**, main symptoms, medical conditions, and any medicines you take, I can help you choose the safest OTC option.
